about: A frozen snapshot of DSAverse page descriptions, used as the RAG and Vector Search corpus.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: N-Queens
docs.text: N-Queens. Place N queens on an N×N chessboard so no two attack each other. Backtracking places queens row by row, pruning columns and diagonals that would cause conflicts.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Rat in a Maze
docs.text: Rat in a Maze. Navigate a rat from the top-left to bottom-right of a binary maze grid. Backtracking explores all paths, marking cells visited and unmarking them when a dead end is hit.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Word Search
docs.text: Word Search. Find a word in a 2D character grid by exploring all four directions from each cell. Backtracking un-marks visited cells when a path fails, enabling complete search.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Linked List: Circular
docs.text: Linked List: Circular. Tail's next wraps to head — no NULL. Ideal for round-robin and circular buffers.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Linked List: Circular Doubly
docs.text: Linked List: Circular Doubly. Bidirectional + circular — the most powerful variant. No NULL pointers anywhere.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Linked List: Doubly
docs.text: Linked List: Doubly. Bidirectional nodes with prev + next pointers. O(1) tail delete and backward traversal.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: List: Dynamic Array
docs.text: List: Dynamic Array. Resizable array that doubles capacity when full. O(1) access.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: List: Linked List
docs.text: List: Linked List. Dynamic nodes with pointers. Efficient head insert/delete.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Queue: Array
docs.text: Queue: Array. FIFO with circular array. Enqueue at rear, dequeue at front.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Queue: Linked List
docs.text: Queue: Linked List. FIFO with front+rear pointers. True O(1) for both ends.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Stack: Array
docs.text: Stack: Array. LIFO with fixed-size array. Push, pop, and peek in O(1).

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Stack: Linked List
docs.text: Stack: Linked List. LIFO using dynamic linked nodes. No overflow — grows with memory.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Count Set Bits
docs.text: Count Set Bits. Count the number of 1-bits in an integer using Brian Kernighan's algorithm. Each iteration n & (n−1) clears the lowest set bit, running in O(set bits) time.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Power of Two
docs.text: Power of Two. Check whether a number is a power of two using the elegant n & (n−1) == 0 trick. Powers of two have exactly one set bit — flipping it produces zero.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Single Number (XOR)
docs.text: Single Number (XOR). Find the one element that appears only once in an array where every other element appears twice. XOR cancels duplicate pairs in a single linear pass.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Binomial Theorem
docs.text: Binomial Theorem. Expand (a + b)ⁿ by picking a or b from each factor, and see why the coefficients are C(n, k) — with (a + b)³ as a cube cut into 8 blocks.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Combinations
docs.text: Combinations. List every ordered pick, then gather the k! orderings of each set into one row. What is left is nCr.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Counting Principle
docs.text: Counting Principle. A decision tree that grows one stage at a time: every choice multiplies the leaves. Then the addition rule for either-or cases.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Inclusion-Exclusion
docs.text: Inclusion-Exclusion. Count a union of overlapping sets by adding, subtracting and adding back — with a tally on every Venn region so nothing is counted twice.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Pascal's Triangle
docs.text: Pascal's Triangle. Build each row by adding the two numbers above. Find C(n, k), its mirror image, the hockey stick and the row sums of 2ⁿ.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Permutations
docs.text: Permutations. Fill k slots from n items and watch the choices shrink — n, n − 1, n − 2 — or stay at n when repeats are allowed.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Pigeonhole Principle
docs.text: Pigeonhole Principle. More pigeons than holes forces a collision. Then a surprise: in any group, two people have shaken the same number of hands.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Stars and Bars
docs.text: Stars and Bars. Share n identical items among k bins by dragging k − 1 bars through a row of stars. Every arrangement is one distribution.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: ARP and Switching
docs.text: ARP and Switching. An ARP request is broadcast and answered, and a switch learns which MAC lives on which port: flood while the destination is unknown, forward once learned.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Distance Vector Routing
docs.text: Distance Vector Routing. Routers trade distance tables Bellman-Ford style until they converge — then a link fails, bad news counts to infinity, and poison reverse steps in.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: DNS Resolution
docs.text: DNS Resolution. A stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, which walks root, TLD and authoritative servers — then answers the next lookup from cache until the TTL runs out.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
docs.text: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3. Head-of-line blocking three ways: queued responses in HTTP/1.1, one lost TCP segment stalling every HTTP/2 stream, and QUIC isolating streams over UDP.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Link State Routing
docs.text: Link State Routing. Link-state advertisements flood the network until every router holds the same map, and each one runs Dijkstra for its own forwarding table.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: OSI and TCP/IP Layers
docs.text: OSI and TCP/IP Layers. A message travels down the stack gaining a header per layer, crosses the wire as bits, and is unwrapped layer by layer on the way up.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Sliding Window Protocols
docs.text: Sliding Window Protocols. Stop-and-Wait, Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat with packets and ACKs in flight, losses you inject, timeouts and a window that slides.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Subnetting and CIDR
docs.text: Subnetting and CIDR. An IPv4 address as 32 bits under a mask: network and broadcast addresses, the usable host range, and whether two hosts share a subnet.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: TCP Congestion Control
docs.text: TCP Congestion Control. cwnd plotted round by round: slow start, ssthresh, additive increase and multiplicative decrease, and why Reno treats three duplicate ACKs gentler than a timeout.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: TCP Handshake
docs.text: TCP Handshake. SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK with real sequence numbers, both endpoints walking their state machines, then the FIN teardown and TIME_WAIT.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Join Algorithms
docs.text: Join Algorithms. Nested-loop, hash join and sort-merge join on the same two tables, counting every comparison to see which one wins and why.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: LSM Trees
docs.text: LSM Trees. Writes land in a memtable, flush to immutable SSTables and compact into larger levels; reads check newest first and skip tables with Bloom filters.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: MVCC
docs.text: MVCC. Every update writes a new version. Each transaction reads from its own snapshot, readers never block writers, and old versions wait for garbage collection.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Normalization
docs.text: Normalization. A messy table, its functional dependencies and its update, insert and delete anomalies — then the table splitting apart through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Relational Algebra
docs.text: Relational Algebra. Selection, projection, join, union, difference and rename on small tables, evaluating an expression tree from the leaves up.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Serializability
docs.text: Serializability. Find the conflicting operations in a schedule, draw the precedence graph edge by edge, and read the equivalent serial order off it — unless there is a cycle.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: SQL Query Order
docs.text: SQL Query Order. Rows flowing through FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY and LIMIT in logical order — which is why a SELECT alias cannot appear in WHERE.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Transaction Isolation Levels
docs.text: Transaction Isolation Levels. Two transactions on one timeline. Switch from Read Uncommitted to Serializable and watch dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms and lost updates disappear.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Two-Phase Locking
docs.text: Two-Phase Locking. Shared and exclusive locks in a lock table: a growing phase, a lock point, a shrinking phase — and the deadlocks and cascading aborts that strict 2PL deals with.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Write-Ahead Logging
docs.text: Write-Ahead Logging. Log records with LSNs are forced to disk before the pages they describe. Then the power fails, and recovery redoes history and undoes the losers.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Derivative Rules
docs.text: Derivative Rules. The power rule, the product rule as a rectangle growing on two sides, and the chain rule as rates multiplying through a composition.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Gradient Descent
docs.text: Gradient Descent. A ball stepping downhill on a loss surface in 3D and on its contour map. Slide the learning rate from crawling to converging to zigzagging to blowing up.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Graphing with Derivatives
docs.text: Graphing with Derivatives. f, f′ and f″ stacked on one x-axis. Rising and falling, bending up and down, maxima, minima and inflection points, all tied together.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Limits. Walk towards a point from the left and from the right. A removable hole, a jump and an asymptote, then an ε–δ band you can tighten.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Newton's Method
docs.text: Newton's Method. Follow the tangent down to the x-axis, then do it again. Correct digits double each step near a root — until a bad start sends it cycling or flying off.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Optimization
docs.text: Optimization. Cut squares from the corners of a sheet and fold it into an open box. Which cut holds the most? Find it where the tangent goes flat.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Partial Derivatives and Gradients
docs.text: Partial Derivatives and Gradients. Slice a surface along x and along y to get the two partial slopes, then see the gradient on the contour map — always perpendicular to the level curves.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Taylor Series
docs.text: Taylor Series. Add one term at a time and watch the polynomial hug sin x and eˣ. For ln(1 + x), see exactly where adding terms stops helping.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: The Derivative
docs.text: The Derivative. A secant line through two points of a curve, pulled together until it becomes the tangent — with the difference quotient updating live.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Binary Search — Decision Tree
docs.text: Binary Search — Decision Tree. See each comparison as a branch in a decision tree — left for smaller, right for larger, until found or eliminated.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Closest Pair of Points
docs.text: Closest Pair of Points. Geometric D&C: divide the point set by a vertical line, recurse on halves, then check the δ-wide strip for cross-half pairs.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Merge Sort — Recursion Tree
docs.text: Merge Sort — Recursion Tree. Watch the recursive split tree grow downward, then see sorted subarrays merge back up level by level.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Strassen's Matrix Multiplication
docs.text: Strassen's Matrix Multiplication. Step through all 7 sub-matrix multiplications that replace the naive 8, and watch the result matrix assemble.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: 0/1 Knapsack
docs.text: 0/1 Knapsack. Classic optimization problem using 2D DP to maximize total value within a weight capacity, where each item can be taken at most once.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Edit Distance
docs.text: Edit Distance. Minimum number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions to transform one string into another. Foundation of spell checkers and autocorrect.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Fibonacci Numbers
docs.text: Fibonacci Numbers. Classic example of memoization transforming exponential time complexity into linear by caching previously computed values in the recursion tree.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: House Robber
docs.text: House Robber. Maximize money robbed from a street of houses with the constraint that no two adjacent houses can be robbed. Elegant 1D DP solution.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Longest Common Subsequence
docs.text: Longest Common Subsequence. 2D DP table approach to find the longest subsequence common to two strings. Foundation for diff tools, version control, and DNA analysis.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
docs.text: Longest Increasing Subsequence. Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence in an array. Can be solved in O(n²) with DP or O(n log n) with patience sorting.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Making Change
docs.text: Making Change. Find the minimum number of coins needed to make a target amount using bottom-up tabulation. Classic unbounded knapsack pattern.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Matrix Chain Multiplication
docs.text: Matrix Chain Multiplication. Find the optimal parenthesization of a matrix chain to minimize scalar multiplications. Classic interval DP — the table fills diagonally by chain length.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Maximum Subarray
docs.text: Maximum Subarray. Kadane's algorithm finds the contiguous subarray with maximum sum in linear time — a beautiful example of optimized DP.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Breadth-First Search
docs.text: Breadth-First Search. Explores a graph level by level, visiting all neighbors of a node before moving to the next level. Uses a queue and guarantees shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Connected Components
docs.text: Connected Components. Identifies all groups of nodes that are connected to each other in an undirected graph. Can be found using BFS or DFS.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Depth-First Search
docs.text: Depth-First Search. Explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. Uses a stack (or recursion) and is the foundation for cycle detection, topological sort, and more.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Dijkstra's Shortest Path
docs.text: Dijkstra's Shortest Path. Finds the shortest path from a source node to all other nodes in a weighted graph with non-negative edges. Uses a greedy approach with a priority queue.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Floyd-Warshall
docs.text: Floyd-Warshall. Finds shortest paths between all pairs of nodes in a weighted graph. Uses dynamic programming and works with negative weights (but not negative cycles).

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Kruskal's MST
docs.text: Kruskal's MST. Finds the minimum spanning tree by sorting all edges by weight and greedily adding edges that don't create a cycle. Uses Union-Find data structure.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Prim's Minimum Spanning Tree
docs.text: Prim's Minimum Spanning Tree. Finds the minimum spanning tree of a weighted undirected graph using a greedy algorithm. Starts from an arbitrary node and grows the tree by adding the cheapest edge.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Topological Sort (DFS)
docs.text: Topological Sort (DFS). DFS-based topological ordering: run DFS and push each node to a stack on completion. Reverse of the completion order gives a valid topological ordering.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Topological Sort
docs.text: Topological Sort. Orders nodes in a Directed Acyclic Graph such that every directed edge goes from earlier to later in the ordering. Essential for task scheduling and dependency resolution.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Binomial Queues
docs.text: Binomial Queues. Forest of binomial trees with unique ranks. Merging works like binary addition — two trees of the same rank merge into one of the next rank.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Fibonacci Heaps
docs.text: Fibonacci Heaps. Lazy heap where insert adds a singleton tree to the root list. Consolidation is deferred until extract-min, giving O(1) amortized insert and decrease-key.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Heaps
docs.text: Heaps. Complete binary tree with heap property — parent is always ≥ (max-heap) or ≤ (min-heap) its children. Array-based implementation with O(1) peek.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Leftist Heaps
docs.text: Leftist Heaps. Binary heap where npl(left) ≥ npl(right) at every node. The right spine is kept short (O(log n)), and all operations reduce to a single merge primitive.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Skew Heaps
docs.text: Skew Heaps. Self-adjusting version of the leftist heap. No npl stored — children are unconditionally swapped on every merge step, achieving amortized O(log n) without bookkeeping.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: B+ Trees
docs.text: B+ Trees. The database index: all values live in linked leaves, so range scans walk sideways instead of back up the tree.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: B Trees
docs.text: B Trees. Wide nodes that keep the tree shallow, splitting and promoting keys upward so every leaf stays the same depth.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Closed Hash Tables
docs.text: Closed Hash Tables. Open addressing: every key lives in the table itself, probing forward until it finds a free slot.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Closed Hash Tables with Buckets
docs.text: Closed Hash Tables with Buckets. Each slot is a small fixed bucket — fewer probes, better cache behaviour, and an overflow area when a bucket fills.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Open Hash Tables
docs.text: Open Hash Tables. Separate chaining: every slot holds a list, so collisions extend a chain instead of hunting for space.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Radix Tree
docs.text: Radix Tree. A trie with single-child chains collapsed into one edge, cutting the node count on sparse key sets.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Red-Black Trees
docs.text: Red-Black Trees. Balance by colouring rather than strict height, trading slightly taller trees for cheaper inserts.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Splay Trees
docs.text: Splay Trees. Self-adjusting tree that rotates every accessed node to the root, making hot keys progressively cheaper.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Ternary Search Tree
docs.text: Ternary Search Tree. A trie-BST hybrid: three children per node instead of one per alphabet symbol, trading speed for memory.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Area Between Curves
docs.text: Area Between Curves. Find where two curves meet, then add up thin strips of height top minus bottom — splitting the range wherever the curves swap places.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
docs.text: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Sweep the right edge of an area along the axis and plot how much has accumulated. The slope of that curve at every x is exactly f(x).

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Integration by Parts
docs.text: Integration by Parts. Trace the curve (u, v) and the rectangle under its end point splits into two regions: ∫u dv on one side of the curve and ∫v du on the other.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Integration by Substitution
docs.text: Integration by Substitution. Change the variable and the axis stretches: each thin strip gets wider by u′(x) and shorter by the same factor, so the area survives intact.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Numerical Integration
docs.text: Numerical Integration. Trapezoids, midpoints and Simpson's parabolas side by side. Double n and the errors fall by 4, 4 and 16 — straight lines on a log scale.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Riemann Sums
docs.text: Riemann Sums. Fill the area under a curve with rectangles — left, right or midpoint — and watch the error shrink as the rectangles get thinner.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: The Definite Integral
docs.text: The Definite Integral. The limit of Riemann sums is a signed area: pieces above the axis count positive, pieces below count negative.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Volumes of Revolution
docs.text: Volumes of Revolution. Spin a region around an axis in 3D. Slice the solid into disks or washers, add up their volumes, and watch the total converge on a cone, a sphere or a paraboloid.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Change of Basis
docs.text: Change of Basis. One vector, two coordinate grids. The basis matrix converts one way and its inverse converts back.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Determinant
docs.text: Determinant. The factor by which a matrix scales area in 2D and volume in 3D. Negative means flipped; zero means squashed flat.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues
docs.text: Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues. Sweep a vector around the circle and light up the ones that stay on their own line. The eigenvalue is how much they stretch.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Gaussian Elimination
docs.text: Gaussian Elimination. Row operations reduce a 3×3 system step by step, while three planes in 3D keep meeting at the same point — or never meet, or share a line.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Inverse Matrices
docs.text: Inverse Matrices. Row-reduce [A | I] until the left side is I and the right side is A⁻¹, then watch A⁻¹ put the plane back where it was.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Least Squares
docs.text: Least Squares. Fit a line to points you can drag. The best fit is a projection onto the column space, and the residuals stand perpendicular to it.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Linear Combinations and Span
docs.text: Linear Combinations and Span. Scale two vectors and add them. Every point you can reach is their span — the whole plane, or a single line when the vectors line up.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Matrix as a Transformation
docs.text: Matrix as a Transformation. A matrix moves the whole plane, and its columns say exactly where î and ĵ land. Drag them and watch the grid follow.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Matrix Multiplication
docs.text: Matrix Multiplication. Row times column for the numbers, and one transformation after another for the picture — which is why AB and BA differ.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Rank and Null Space
docs.text: Rank and Null Space. A matrix that squashes 3D space onto a plane or a line, the vectors it sends to zero, and why the two always add up to three.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Banker's Algorithm
docs.text: Banker's Algorithm. Allocation, Max, Need and Available — the safety check that finds a safe sequence before any request is granted.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: CPU Scheduling
docs.text: CPU Scheduling. FCFS, SJF, SRTF and Priority on the same workload — watch the Gantt chart grow and the average waiting time move.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Deadlock Detection
docs.text: Deadlock Detection. Collapse a resource-allocation graph into a wait-for graph and walk it for a cycle, with the four Coffman conditions on screen.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Dining Philosophers
docs.text: Dining Philosophers. Five philosophers grab their left fork and deadlock. Number the forks, take the lower one first, and the cycle cannot close.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Disk Scheduling
docs.text: Disk Scheduling. FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK and C-LOOK plotted as head movement across the cylinders, with total seek distance.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Memory Allocation
docs.text: Memory Allocation. First, best, worst and next fit carving holes in memory until a request fails with enough space free — then compaction.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Page Replacement
docs.text: Page Replacement. FIFO, LRU and Optimal deciding which frame to evict — including the reference string where more frames cause more faults.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Producer-Consumer
docs.text: Producer-Consumer. A bounded buffer guarded by empty, full and mutex semaphores — producers and consumers blocking and waking each other.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text: Race Conditions. Two threads run counter++ as load, add, store. Explore all twenty interleavings, then make them all correct with a mutex.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Round Robin Scheduling
docs.text: Round Robin Scheduling. A ready queue that cycles every time quantum. Shrink the quantum and response improves while context switches pile up.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Bayes' Theorem
docs.text: Bayes' Theorem. A thousand people, a rare condition and a good test. Slide the base rate, sensitivity and false-positive rate and see why most positives are false alarms.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Binomial Distribution
docs.text: Binomial Distribution. Balls bounce left or right through a Galton board and pile up in bins. The pile takes the shape of C(n, k) pᵏ (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ — change n and p and drop more.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Birthday Paradox
docs.text: Birthday Paradox. With only 23 people the chance of a shared birthday passes 50%. The exact curve against a seeded simulation, and the pairs that explain it.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Central Limit Theorem
docs.text: Central Limit Theorem. Draw samples from a lopsided distribution and average each one. The averages pile up into a bell curve whose width shrinks as σ / √n.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Conditional Probability
docs.text: Conditional Probability. Knowing B happened shrinks the sample space to B. See it on the dice grid, then drag the splits of an area model and watch P(A | B) change.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Law of Large Numbers
docs.text: Law of Large Numbers. Roll a die thousands of times and track the running average. It wanders at first, then settles on 3.5 inside a band that narrows like 1 / √n.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Normal Distribution
docs.text: Normal Distribution. Slide μ and σ, drag two points along the axis, and read off the area between them. The 68–95–99.7 rule and z-scores fall out of one curve.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Random Variables and Expectation
docs.text: Random Variables and Expectation. A distribution as bars on a beam. The expected value is where it balances, and the variance measures how far the weight sits from that point. Drag the bars.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Sample Spaces and Events
docs.text: Sample Spaces and Events. All 36 rolls of two dice on one grid and the 8 paths of three coins. Events are sets of outcomes — highlight them, then take unions, intersections and complements.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Factorial
docs.text: Factorial. Calculate factorial using recursive function calls to understand base cases and the call stack building up and unwinding.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Fibonacci Sequence
docs.text: Fibonacci Sequence. Compute Fibonacci numbers showing explosive naive recursion vs efficient memoization — see the dramatic call count difference.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Maze Solver
docs.text: Maze Solver. Navigate a maze using backtracking — explore paths, hit dead ends, retreat, and try again until the goal is found.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: N-Queens Problem
docs.text: N-Queens Problem. Place N queens on an NxN chessboard using backtracking — explore and undo choices systematically until solutions are found.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Permutations
docs.text: Permutations. Generate all n! permutations using swap-based backtracking — fix positions left-to-right and swap back to explore every arrangement.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: String Reversal
docs.text: String Reversal. Reverse a string character by character using recursive divide & conquer — watch the result build on the unwind phase.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Subsets (Power Set)
docs.text: Subsets (Power Set). Generate all 2ⁿ subsets via binary include/exclude decisions — watch the full decision tree grow level by level.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Sudoku Solver
docs.text: Sudoku Solver. Solve a 9×9 Sudoku grid using constraint-based backtracking — place digits, hit dead ends, erase, and try the next candidate.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Tower of Hanoi
docs.text: Tower of Hanoi. Solve the classic puzzle using elegant divide & conquer — three recursive steps that together achieve what seems impossible.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Binary Search
docs.text: Binary Search. Repeatedly halves the search space by comparing the target with the midpoint element. The gold standard for searching sorted arrays.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Block Search
docs.text: Block Search. Scans block endpoints in steps of √n to identify the correct block, then searches linearly within it. Also known as Jump Search.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Exponential Search
docs.text: Exponential Search. Doubles the bound (1 → 2 → 4 → 8 …) to find a range where the target lies, then applies binary search within that range.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Fibonacci Search
docs.text: Fibonacci Search. Divides the array using Fibonacci numbers. Avoids division entirely — uses only addition and subtraction to compute probe positions.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Interpolation Search
docs.text: Interpolation Search. Estimates the target's position using value proportions — like looking up a name in a phone book. Excels on uniformly distributed data.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Jump Search
docs.text: Jump Search. Jumps ahead in steps of √n to find the right block, then scans linearly within that block. A practical middle-ground between linear and binary.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Linear Search
docs.text: Linear Search. Sequential scan through every element until the target is found. Works on any array — sorted or unsorted — and finds all occurrences in one pass.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Ternary Search
docs.text: Ternary Search. Splits the range into three equal thirds using two midpoints, eliminating one third per iteration. An interesting theoretical variant of binary search.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Bubble Sort
docs.text: Bubble Sort. Simple comparison-based algorithm that repeatedly steps through the list, compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they're in the wrong order.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Bucket Sort
docs.text: Bucket Sort. Distributes elements into a fixed number of buckets based on value range, sorts each bucket individually, then concatenates the results.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Heap Sort
docs.text: Heap Sort. Uses a binary max heap data structure to sort elements by repeatedly extracting the maximum and placing it in sorted position.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Insertion Sort
docs.text: Insertion Sort. Builds the sorted array one element at a time by inserting each element into its correct position in the already-sorted portion.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Merge Sort
docs.text: Merge Sort. Divide and conquer algorithm that splits the array into halves, recursively sorts each half, then merges them back in sorted order.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Quick Sort
docs.text: Quick Sort. Efficient divide and conquer algorithm that partitions the array around a pivot, placing elements smaller than the pivot to its left.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Radix Sort
docs.text: Radix Sort. Non-comparison based sorting that processes individual digits from least to most significant, using counting sort as a subroutine.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Selection Sort
docs.text: Selection Sort. Finds the minimum element from the unsorted portion and places it at the beginning, reducing the unsorted region in each pass.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: KMP String Matching
docs.text: KMP String Matching. Knuth-Morris-Pratt avoids redundant comparisons by pre-computing a failure function. When a mismatch occurs, the pattern shifts by the maximum safe amount rather than just one position.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Rabin-Karp
docs.text: Rabin-Karp. Uses a rolling hash to compare a sliding window of the text with the pattern in O(1) per step. Hash collisions trigger a character-by-character verification.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Z-Algorithm
docs.text: Z-Algorithm. Computes the Z-array where Z[i] is the length of the longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of the string. Enables linear-time pattern matching without a separate failure function.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: AVL Tree
docs.text: AVL Tree. Self-balancing BST that uses rotations (LL, RR, LR, RL) to keep height at O(log n).

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Binary Search Tree
docs.text: Binary Search Tree. Insert, search, and delete nodes while maintaining the BST ordering property.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Binary Tree Traversals
docs.text: Binary Tree Traversals. Visualize Inorder, Preorder, Postorder, and Level-Order traversals with a live call-stack panel.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Segment Tree
docs.text: Segment Tree. Range queries and point updates in O(log n) by partitioning the array into tree segments.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Trie
docs.text: Trie. Prefix tree for fast word insert, search, and autocomplete — each edge is one character.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: 3Sum
docs.text: 3Sum. Sort the array, fix a pivot, then run a two-pointer sweep on the remainder. Duplicate pivots and duplicate pairs are skipped to produce a unique set of triplets.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Container With Most Water
docs.text: Container With Most Water. Given bar heights, find two bars that trap the most water. Two pointers converge inward, always moving the shorter bar — watch the water area update in real time.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
docs.text: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters. Expand the window rightward adding new characters; shrink from the left whenever a duplicate is detected. The window always holds a valid unique-character substring.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Maximum Sum Subarray
docs.text: Maximum Sum Subarray. Find the contiguous subarray of length k with the largest sum using a fixed-size sliding window that shifts one position at a time.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Minimum Window Substring
docs.text: Minimum Window Substring. Expand the right pointer until the window contains all required characters, then shrink from the left to find the tightest valid window. Track character frequencies to detect validity in O(1).

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Two Sum II
docs.text: Two Sum II. Classic two-pointer technique on a sorted array. Place one pointer at each end and converge inward, eliminating half the search space at every step.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Valid Palindrome
docs.text: Valid Palindrome. Verify a string reads the same forwards and backwards by comparing characters from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric characters.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Async Await and Event Loop
docs.text: Async Await and Event Loop. The event loop as a spinning wheel. Task queues, microtask vs macrotask, how await suspends a coroutine without blocking the thread.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Classes Objects and Memory
docs.text: Classes Objects and Memory. How classes and instances live in memory. Python __dict__, __class__ pointer, method lookup chain, and metaclasses.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Composition vs Inheritance
docs.text: Composition vs Inheritance. "Is-a" vs "has-a". Fragile base class problem animated. Why swapping a component is impossible with deep inheritance but trivial with composition.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: C++ Execution Pipeline
docs.text: C++ Execution Pipeline. Preprocessor → Compiler → Assembler → Linker → Loader → CPU. See why compiled code runs 50× faster than Python.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: CPU Cache Hierarchy
docs.text: CPU Cache Hierarchy. L1/L2/L3 cache lines, spatial locality, cache misses vs hits, and why column-major array access kills performance.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Floating Point and IEEE 754
docs.text: Floating Point and IEEE 754. Why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 — binary fractions, the 64-bit layout, round-to-nearest-even, ULP spacing, cancellation and NaN.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Garbage Collection
docs.text: Garbage Collection. Reference counting, cyclic GC, mark-and-sweep, and generational collection. How memory gets reclaimed automatically.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: How a Database Query Executes
docs.text: How a Database Query Executes. SQL → Parser → Planner → Optimizer → Executor. Index scan vs full scan animated. Why the query planner chooses what it chooses.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: How a File System Works
docs.text: How a File System Works. Blocks, inodes, directory entries, path resolution, hard links vs symlinks, the page cache, and journaling for crash consistency.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: How a REST API Works
docs.text: How a REST API Works. HTTP verbs, status codes, request/response cycle, JSON serialization, authentication headers, and REST constraints visualized.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: How Containers Work
docs.text: How Containers Work. Namespaces, cgroups and overlay layers — why a container is just a process, and how it differs from a VM.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: How Git Works Internally
docs.text: How Git Works Internally. Blob, tree, and commit objects. SHA-1 content addressing. Branches as sticky notes on commits. Merge vs rebase as DAG transformations.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: How the Browser Renders a Page
docs.text: How the Browser Renders a Page. HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, compositing. Why transform animates at 60fps and top does not.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: How the Internet Routes a Packet
docs.text: How the Internet Routes a Packet. Subnet masks, ARP, NAT, longest prefix match, TTL and BGP — no packet ever knows its own route.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: HTTPS and TLS
docs.text: HTTPS and TLS. Certificate chains, Diffie-Hellman key exchange, the paint-mixing analogy, and why TLS 1.3 needs only 1 round trip.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Inheritance and MRO
docs.text: Inheritance and MRO. C3 linearization step by step. Why MRO exists (diamond problem), how super() walks the chain, and what multiple inheritance really does.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: JIT Compilation
docs.text: JIT Compilation. Profiling counters finding hot code, tiered compilation, inline caches, speculative optimization with guards, and deoptimization.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Multithreading
docs.text: Multithreading. Thread creation, time slicing, race conditions, mutex locks, and deadlock — each animated with the classic counter and dining philosophers examples.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Polymorphism and Virtual Dispatch
docs.text: Polymorphism and Virtual Dispatch. C++ vtables in memory. How virtual function calls follow the vptr → vtable → function pointer chain. Non-virtual vs virtual call cost.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Processes vs Threads
docs.text: Processes vs Threads. Virtual address spaces, the process control block, fork() semantics, and why threads share heap but not stack.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Python Execution Pipeline
docs.text: Python Execution Pipeline. Source → Tokens → AST → Bytecode → CPython VM → Memory Model → GIL. Every layer visualized step by step.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Python Memory Model
docs.text: Python Memory Model. PyObject internals, reference counting, the small int cache, closures, and LEGB name resolution — all animated.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: System Calls and Kernel Mode
docs.text: System Calls and Kernel Mode. Protection rings, the syscall trap instruction, table dispatch, copy_from_user validation, and why buffered I/O exists.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Unicode and UTF-8
docs.text: Unicode and UTF-8. Code points, UTF-8 prefix bits, UTF-16 surrogate pairs, grapheme clusters and ZWJ emoji — and why string length lies.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: Virtual Memory and Paging
docs.text: Virtual Memory and Paging. Virtual address space layout, page tables, TLB, page faults, and why every process thinks it has 4GB of RAM.

docs.subject: cs-core
docs.title: What Happens When You Search a URL
docs.text: What Happens When You Search a URL. DNS resolution → TCP handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request → server pipeline → HTTP response → browser rendering. All 8 acts animated.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Path Compression
docs.text: Path Compression. After find(x), point every node on the path directly to the root. Trees flatten dramatically. Amortised cost approaches O(α(n)) — nearly constant.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Quick Find
docs.text: Quick Find. Store a component ID per element. find() is O(1) — just return id[x]. union() is O(n) — scan the entire array and relabel.

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Quick Union
docs.text: Quick Union. Store a parent pointer per element. union() is O(1) — just repoint one root. find() follows parent links to the root — O(n) worst case (tall trees).

docs.subject: dsa
docs.title: Union by Rank
docs.text: Union by Rank. Always attach the shorter tree under the taller one. Rank tracks tree height. Combined with path compression this is the optimal Union-Find.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Cross Product
docs.text: Cross Product. In 3D, a × b stands perpendicular to both, as long as the parallelogram they span is large — and flips when the order does.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Dot Product
docs.text: Dot Product. One vector's shadow on another, times its length. Its sign says same direction, perpendicular or opposite.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Lines and Planes in 3D
docs.text: Lines and Planes in 3D. A line from a point and a direction, a plane from a point and a normal, where the two meet, and how far a point is from a plane.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Norms and Unit Vectors
docs.text: Norms and Unit Vectors. Three ways to measure length — taxicab, straight-line and largest component — and the unit "circles" each one draws.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Vector Addition and Scaling
docs.text: Vector Addition and Scaling. Tip to tail, the parallelogram rule, stretching and flipping with a scalar, and subtraction as adding the opposite.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Vector Projection
docs.text: Vector Projection. Drop a perpendicular onto a line in 2D, then onto a plane in 3D. What is left over is always at right angles.

docs.subject: math
docs.title: Vectors and Coordinates
docs.text: Vectors and Coordinates. An arrow and a list of numbers are the same thing. Drag the tip and the components change; type the components and the arrow moves.
